item.content:encoded:
The second base position is in rougher shape than I initially thought. There is useful depth available here for 2027, but it is light on real difference makers. And that is largely because of who isn't going to be eligible at second base.
C.J. Abrams won't be, at least to start, though he does seem very likely as of now to end up eligible at second base pretty early on in the season. That is, unfortunately, less true for the likes of Sal Stewart and Otto Lopez, two of the biggest breakout stars at the position, though for opposite reasons; Stewart because he just isn't good enough defensively to justify much time there, Lopez because he's probably too good at shortstop to move back to the keystone. You have something similar with Luis Garcia Jr. (likely just a first baseman moving forward) and Ceddanne Rafaela (too good in center field to play him anywhere else).
And they aren't the only ones losing eligibility for 2027. Curtis Mead, Casey Schmitt, Brooks Lee, Royce Lewis, and Zack Gelof were all at least useful starters at second base in 2026, and none of them played there enough to retain eligibility. Gelof's is the most frustrating case, because he played his 19th game at second base in late August and never appeared there again, coming just one appearance short of retaining eligibility. Even if you're skeptical of his 2026 breakout (as I am), losing him hurts the position.
Right now, I'd say there are maybe six second basemen I feel very good about as my starter for 2026, and then another few who seem like decent starters, and then a whole bunch of useful, but ultimately replaceable options. Does that mean second base is where we should play the positional scarcity game?
Well, if you are the type of Fantasy player who cares about such things, go for it. Second base looks like clearly the weakest position in Fantasy (non-catcher, anyway) for 2027, both in terms of impact bats and viable starting options. So, if you want to nudge Fernando Tatis up a few spots in your overall rankings to ensure you get elite production out of that lineup spot, go for it.
I don't really care all that much about positional scarcity, so I won't be doing much waiting there. I don't mind targeting Tatis in the first round, obviously, but the fact that he is second base eligible only plays a small factor. In part, that's because I just don't care that much about positional scarcity in drafts – we aren't as good as we think we are at projecting which positions will actually be weak and which will be strong in any given season, so I'll just try to draft the best players and not worry too much about which position they'll slot in at.
But I also don't care too much about positional scarcity at second base because plenty of guys unexpectedly gain eligibility there all of the time. Of all infield positions, it is the one where teams seem most willing to just toss a guy out there and see if they can handle it. Don't have enough range for shortstop or enough arm for third base? Get ready to learn second base, buddy.
Which is to say, second base is never actually as bad as it looks. Some hotshot shortstop prospect will probably find himself starting at second base on Opening Day that we can't see coming right now, or some veteran will find himself pushed there based on how his team's offseason goes. It happens every year, and while you probably shouldn't plan your draft around being able to plug someone in at second base unexpectedly, you surely will end up with more options than you expect once the games start. That's just the nature of the position.
For more on the state of the second base position, .
2026 Second Base Review
- Fernando Tatis Jr., SDP: .289 - 96 - 25 - 83 - 38
- Brice Turang, MIL: .268 - 102 - 21 - 100 - 19
- Brandon Lowe, PIT: .260 - 94 - 35 - 96 - 2
- Otto Lopez, MIA: .305 - 94 - 11 - 71 - 34
- Luis García Jr., NYY: .277 - 69 - 30 - 92 - 5
- Ceddanne Rafaela, BOS: .285 - 67 - 16 - 70 - 17
- Kody Clemens, MIN: .239 - 74 - 27 - 81 - 10
- Jazz Chisholm Jr., NYY: .231 - 69 - 19 - 55 - 41
- Luke Keaschall, MIN: .282 - 86 - 10 - 52 - 20
- Luis Arraez, PHI: .310 - 67 - 6 - 64 - 10
- Bryson Stott, PHI: .256 - 71 - 10 - 67 - 27
- Zack Gelof, ATH: .256 - 76 - 22 - 55 - 16
If we remove the players who won't be second base eligible in 2027, Ketel Marte, Ozzie Albies, Ezequiel Duran, and Nick Gonzales slide into the top 12. Which kind of highlights the point about the position: There were plenty of useful options, but few true difference makers. The replacement level at second base tends to be pretty high. However, the difference between, say, the 10th-best option at the position in 2026 and the 20th was a little under $3 in value in the FanGraphs Player Rater – at shortstop, the difference between No. 10 and No. 20 was closer to $5, for example.
Biggest Breakout from 2026
Otto Lopez, Marlins
Lopez slowed down considerably in the second half of the season but still had the breakout many suspected was lurking. He won't hit .305 ever again, but something like a .280 average, double-digit homers, and 25-plus steals is still valuable from a second baseman. Unfortunately, he won't open next season with second-base eligibility. Unless he gets traded to a team with a very good shortstop, he isn't likely to add it anytime soon. So we'll pivot to …
Kody Clemens, Twins
I guess? Clemens finished as the No. 7 second baseman thanks to a huge power breakout that saw him hit 27 homers. The counting stats beyond that were pretty iffy because he didn't really play against lefties earlier in the season. His .233/.286/.393 line against lefties isn't a disaster, but coming from a 30-year-old with clear defensive limitations, the Twins wouldn't be out of line to spend the offseason at least looking for a platoon partner for him. I think there's a pretty good chance we just saw the best season of Clemens' career. I wouldn't be looking to draft him as a starter in 2027 at this point, but if it looks like he's primed for an everyday role, you could definitely get a Brandon Lowe-esque outcome from him in a best-case scenario.
Biggest Bust from 2026
Yeah, I think we might be done here. There were some signs of life from Altuve immediately after the All-Star break, as he hit .308/.373/.440 in August, but he collapsed back to a sub-.700 OPS in September and hasn't posted an OPS north of .800 in a month since July of 2025. He doesn't really steal bases anymore and the Astros lineup is underwhelming enough that you really don't get much of a boost there. Even at a relatively weak position like second base, it just doesn't look like there's much reason to even draft Altuve in 2027, sadly.
Biggest rankings movers from 2026 to 2027
Up: Brandon Lowe, Free Agent; JJ Wetherholt, Cardinals; Kody Clemens, Twins
I understand why Lowe's price was as low as it was entering 2025, with a long list of injuries that had held him to less than 110 games in three straight seasons. But he played 134 games in 2025 and hit 31 homers, and the Fantasy community responded by only moving him up to around 175th in ADP. And of course, he went out and had an even better season in 2026, so surely his price will rise, right? We'll see where he lands in free agency. Lowe proved he can still be an everyday player and still make a significant impact, and there are few players at any position who give you as big an edge on the competition as Lowe does with homers at second base; Clemens is the only other player eligible at the position for 2027 who had more than 25 homers last season.
Wetherholt's rookie season was mostly a success. A second-half wrist injury saw his production collapse in August and September when he was healthy enough to play, but he was hitting .259/.356/.399 with a 23-homer, 16-steal pace at the All-Star break and he did it as a 23-year-old. I'm not sure there are too many superstar-level outcomes for Wetherholt – that wasn't really projected for him as a prospect, either – but there's enough pop in his bat to project some 25-homer outcomes here, and he could emerge as a 20-steal guy hitting at the top of the lineup, too. The .242 final batting average is a red flag, but with his contact skills, it's not unreasonable to expect something closer to the .275 range as he grows. It's a sneaky-exciting skill set for a guy who might get lost in the shuffle a bit among other, more obviously exciting young bats.
Down: Ketel Marte, Diamondbacks; Nico Hoerner, Cubs; Jose Altuve, Astros; Matt McLain, Reds
Marte's outlook for 2027 is at least somewhat in flux because he seems pretty likely to get traded away after all of the ... weirdness in Arizona. He took a step back in 2026, with his .249/.316/432 line clearly his worst since 2022. The underlying numbers were still plenty strong, if not quite as good as his previous few seasons. That's not unusual for a 32-year-old, and betting on a player multiple years into his 30s to bounce back after a down season is often a surefire way to invite disappointment. But if you go into next season expecting something like a .275 average and 25-plus homers (plus whatever run production his likely new home ballpark and lineup will allow), he should be a fine pick after the first four or so rounds are done.
Hoerner dipping down to just 23 steals in his age-29 season seems like a pretty bad sign. It doesn't mean he can't bounce back, but speed generally fades as a player hits their 30s, and the fact that it was combined with the lowest BABIP Hoerner has posted in any MLB season feels like an especially worrying sign. I don't mind betting on a bounceback when Hoerner will likely come very cheap, but if he isn't hitting near the top of the Cubs lineup, he might just be a Fantasy also-ran even if there is some positive regression; he scored just 62 runs in 2026!
There was some real hype around McLain after a massive Spring Training, which should serve as a reminder that, even with all of the information at our fingertips, your bias should still strongly tilt in the direction of dismissing Spring Training production. McLain still has a mildly intriguing power/speed combination, but after watching him flirt with the Mendoza Line in consecutive seasons, it's clear he just doesn't do enough well to make the 15 or so homers and 20 or so steals worth it.
Offseason preview
Who needs an upgrade most?
One thing to note with the Nationals specifically: They talked about moving C.J. Abrams to second base and played him there a handful of times in the second half of the 2026 season, so that might be a hole they fill internally. Shortstop would likely be filled by Nasim Nunez at first, with Seaver King as a candidate to win the job out of Spring Training and Eli Willits as the likely longer-term option.
Top impending free agents
- Jazz Chisholm
- Brandon Lowe
- Luis Arraez
- Gleyber Torres
A year ago, Chisholm looked like he might be a $200 million man when he hit free agency; now, it feels like a real question whether the Yankees will even extend a qualifying offer to him. He seems extremely likely to end up on the market for a long time before settling for the kind of one-year-plus-an-option contract that has become so common in recent years. He still has a very Fantasy-friendly skill set – 19 homers and 41 steals even in a down season! – but the batting average is actively harmful and the strikeouts really hurt his value in points leagues. I actually like the idea of betting on a bounceback in 2027, but Chisholm's poor contact skills will likely always leave him with a very low floor to worry about.
Trade candidates
- Ketel Marte, Diamondbacks
- Otto Lopez, Marlins
- Ozzie Albies, Braves
- Bryson Stott, Phillies
- Brendan Donovan, Mariners
Albies is a very interesting one, because his contract is still dirt cheap (just $7 million in 2027), but it's not clear he's even worth much more than that at this point. He hasn't been worth more than 1.4 WAR in a season since 2023; he is just 26th in WAR among second basemen since the start of 2025. Entering his age-30 season, is there really much reason to bet on a bounceback? He's cheap enough that the Braves will probably just keep him around, but he also probably isn't good enough for a team that truly aims to contend to keep starting every day, especially with how little they've gotten from the shortstop spot over the past few seasons.
Top 2027 rookies to know
- Michael Arroyo, Mariners
- Demetrio Crisantes, Diamondbacks
- Devin Fitz-Gerald, Nationals
- Max Anderson, tigers
The thing we have to remember is that shortstops end up being overrepresented in prospect rankings, while second- and third-basemen are inherently underrepresented. Shortstop prospects inevitably end up moving off the position at much higher rates than at any other position, so at least some of the big, flashy names at shortstop will move to second base. And that's good news, because the list of top prospects at second base heading into 2026 is pretty underwhelming! But we could see more interesting names like Franklin Arias, Seaver King, Luis Pena, or Leo De Vries end up playing enough second base to qualify there some time in 2027.

item.content:encoded:
Pirates’ Nick Gonzales Positioned to End Year in Exclusive Group of .300 Hitters
Only seven players enter the final day of the 2026 season with a batting average of .300 or better. Pirates infielder Nick Gonzales (.302) is one of them.
Gonzales has a chance to be the first qualified hitter for the Pirates to finish with a batting average of .300 or better since teammate Bryan Reynolds hit .302 in 2021.
While accomplishing the feat would be “cool,” Gonzales is not stepping into the batter’s box thinking about his batting average.
“You just try to be consistent every single day and if that’s where I am, that’s where I am,” he explained. “It’s something that could really eat you up if you really focus on it too much throughout the year. I just play my game and try to be consistent.”
Batting average is considered to be an antiquated stat by some in today’s game. Given Gonzales’ profile and background, he’s someone who sees the value in hitting for average.
“I think it’s still a testament to finding ways to get hits,” he said. “I’m not a guy who’s gonna just swing for home runs. That’s not really my game. So, you gotta kinda learn how to find hits.”
The six other qualified hitters who join Gonzales in the .300 club are the Astros’ Yordan Alvarez (.316), Diamondbacks’ Gabriel Moreno (.311), Phillies’ Luis Arraez (.310), Rays Chandler Simpson (.306), Marlins’ Otto Lopez (.305) and Rockies’ TJ Rumfield (.300).
10 years ago, 25 hitters finished with a .300 batting average. The fact now that so few hitters are able to finish at or above the mark is a testament to the quality of pitchers in today’s game, Gonzales believes.
“I don’t think hitters are worse,” he said. “I think it’s just that the pitching is that good.”
Gonzales’ offensive showing with the Pirates this season has been the best of his career. But while his offense has been a bright spot this season, his defense has lagged well behind.
Gonzales, a natural second baseman, has been tasked with manning a new position. After adding Brandon Lowe at second base in the offseason, the Pirates had to shift Gonzales to third base. The 27-year-old has committed 11 errors in 112 games at the hot corner with minus-15 defensive runs saved.
While Gonzales hasn’t had the year he’s wanted defensively, he’s not allowed his fielding woes to carry over to the plate.
“You don’t take your glove to hit and you don’t take your bat to play defense. So, just flush it. Forget about it,” he explained. “As soon as I step back in the box, it’s over with.”
Through all of the defensive inconsistencies this season, Gonzales has remained a steady presence in the Pirates’ lineup. Finishing the season in what will be an exclusive group of players with a .300 batting average would be a reflection of the progress he’s made offensively this season.
“He should take pride in that, in how he’s been able to swing the bat for us,” said manager Don Kelly. “He’s had some huge at-bats and swung the bat well. He’s been a big part of our offensive success this year.”

item.content:encoded:
PITTSBURGH — The Pittsburgh Pirates won't finish the 2026 season with playoff baseball and it's a let down for every player, especially Paul Skenes.
The Pirates' starting pitcher, who ended his third MLB season, hasn't been a part of a postseason team yet, with the 2026 team eliminated a week ago.
Skenes and the Pirates did avoid a losing season, but the ace is done with coming up short and wants to be a part of a playoff squad, something he envisions in Pittsburgh.
"That's cool. We all wanted to play in October," Skenes said. "Like I said, I think our best baseball is ahead of us, I thought there was a lot of kind of unfortunate stuff that happened this year. Stuff that was just out of our control. Guys getting hurt and stuff like that. I think it'd be a different picture if stuff like that didn't happen. So it's tough.
"This is my third year, and every year, at the end, we’re talking about ‘What’s it going to look like for next year,’ and I’m tired of it. We are in a good position for next year, I know that, but it’s gonna be tough to think about that again for a whole offseason.”
Skenes Hoping For Better in 2027
The Pirates were competitive throughout the 2026 season and can clinch a winning season with a win in their final two games against the Detroit Tigers at Comerica Park, on either Sept. 26 or Sept. 27.
Pittsburgh last had a winning season in 2018, 82-79, and hasn't made the postseason since 2015, the second-longest streak in baseball to the Los Angeles Angels (2014).
The Pirates have had little success in recent history, with this just the fifth non-losing season in the past 34 years, with three postseason appearances from 2013-15 and a record 20 straight losing seasons from 1993-2012.
2026 was a much better season for the Pirates, who put together a roster that had postseason potential.
The Pirates had one of the best lineups in baseball before the All-Star break, with offseason additions in second baseman Brandon Lowe and slugger Ryan O'Hearn excelling, internal improvements from center fielder Oneil Cruz, left fielder Bryan Reynolds, first baseman Spencer Horwitz, catcher Endy Rodríguez and third baseman Nick Gonzales, plus breakout rookies in shortstop Konnor Griffin and right fielder Esmerlyn Valdez.
Pittsburgh fell short of their goal due to injuries to their best hitters, a bullpen that struggled and a starting rotation that was inconsistent.
The Pirates have a much better bullpen following the trade deadline and a starting rotation that should be in a better position next season, so there is reason for optimism that they can finally break through.
"I don't know, and that's going to be another off-season thing," Skenes said about what the Pirates need to do next season. "You know, I don't. I don't think there's anything that needs to be completely overhauled."
Skenes Faces Important Offseason
Skenes has a big offseason, himself, after falling short of his National League Cy Young Award season in 2025.
He posted a 10-11 record in 32 starts, a 3.82 ERA over 174.1. innings pitched, 200 strikeouts to 49 walks, a .227 BAA and a 1.12 WHIP.
Skenes' ERA was almost twice what it was last season, although his expected ERA (3.28) was 10th-best in baseball.
There were some mechanical issues and a drop in velocity for Skenes this season, as well as an early start due to the World Baseball Classic, but with a full offseason ahead of him, he's confident he can fix those issues and help lead the Pirates back to the postseason in 2027.
“I think my best baseball is ahead of me, and I think our best baseball is ahead of us," Skenes said. "Got a long offseason and have the chance to sit down and look at all the stuff. It’s really easy to get emotional and kind of let emotions bleed into some stuff during the season. To be able to sit back and kinda look at the big picture rather than the day-to-day, short-term view of it that takes over in-season, that will be good.”

item.content:encoded:
PITTSBURGH — The Pittsburgh Pirates have benefited greatly from center fielder Oneil Cruz in their lineup, which makes this latest lineup decision perplexing.
Cruz won't start for the Pirates in their next game against the St. Louis Cardinals at PNC Park on Sept. 23, as Jake Mangum takes his place in center field.
It marks the first time Cruz hasn't started a game since Aug. 23 in a 4-0 loss to the Los Angeles Dodgers at Dodger Stadium.
The Pirates won't have Cruz in their lineup for a month and 25 games, so they'll need others to step up.
Why it's Odd Cruz Isn't Starting vs. Cardinals
Pittsburgh faces St. Louis left-handed pitcher Matthew Liberatore in this one, and it's no secret the struggles they've had against southpaws this season.
The Pirates have an 18-32 record against left-handed starting pitching, compared to 62-45 against right-handed pitching.
Cruz has been the Pirates' best hitter against southpaws, batting .323/.373/.476 for an OPS of .849, with 40 hits in 124 at-bats, five doubles, a triple, four home runs and 19 RBI.
He took time this offseason to fix his approach against lefties, working with a left-handed pitcher in batting practice, and it's been a massive improvement, after he hit .102 last season.
Cruz has also been successful against Liberatore this season, with three hits in six at-bats, including a double and an RBI.
The Pirates have hit well against Libertatore in 2026, scoring four runs over 4.2 innings on May 19 and three runs over 5.2 innings on Aug. 30, both at Busch Stadium.
Cruz is more than a month removed from his official return from his left-hand fracture, so he's still dealing with pain.
He's been great since returning, hitting .309/.402/.518 for an OPS of .920 in 30 games, with 34 hits in 110 at-bats, three doubles, a triple, six home runs, 23 RBI and seven stolen bases.
The Pirates are also eliminated from postseason contention, so they can give him a rest day instead of pushing him.
Pirates Lineup vs. Cardinals and Liberatore
| Player | Position | Batting Side |
|---|---|---|
| Konnor Griffin | Shortstop | Right |
| Rafael Flores Jr. | Catcher | Right |
| Bryan Reynolds | Left Fielder | Switch |
| Brandon Lowe | Second Base | Left |
| Nick Gonzales | Designated Hitter | Right |
| Ronny Simon | Right Fielder | Switch |
| Ryan O'Hearn | First Base | Left |
| Jared Triolo | Third Base | Right |
| Jake Mangum | Center Fielder | Switch |
The Pirates have just two left-handed hitters vs. Liberatore, second baseman Brandon Lowe and first baseman Ryan O'Hearn.
Lowe will bat fourth for just the third time this season, last doing so vs. the Dodgers on Aug. 23 and also in an 8-3 win over the Boston Red Sox at PNC Park on Aug. 13.
O'Hearn bats seventh for just the second time this season, first doing it in a 6-5 win over the Kansas City Royals at PNC Park on Sept. 19.
Catcher Rafael Flores Jr. bats second for the first time in his career, the highest he's ever been in an MLB lineup.
Shortstop Konnor Griffin bats leadoff, third baseman Jared Triolo bats seventh and designated hitter Nick Gonzales bats fifth.
Left fielder Bryan Gonzales stays third, right fielder Ronny Simon hits sixth and Mangum bats ninth against the Cardinals.

He would write for Pittsburgh Sports Now after college and has years of experience covering sports across Pittsburgh.

item.content:encoded:
PITTSBURGH — Nick Gonzales has been one of the Pittsburgh Pirates' best hitters, and he could finish as one of the best in baseball.
Gonzales has hit .304/.367/.392 for an OPS of .759 in 141 games for the Pirates, giving him the best batting average and the fourth-best in the National League, with nine games left in the 2026 season.
The Pirates have Gonzales starting at third base in the series opener against the Kansas City Royals at PNC Park on Sept. 18, and it's another chance for him to finish his season strong.
Gonzales also has a realistic chance of winning the NL Batting Title, with Freddy Sanchez the last Pirates player to do so in 2006, batting .344.
Who Gonzales Faces in the NL Batting Title
NL Batting Title Leaders
| Player | Batting Average | Team |
|---|---|---|
| Luis Arraez | .315 | Philadelphia Phillies |
| Gabriel Moreno | .307 | Arizona Diamondbacks |
| Otto Lopez | .306 | Miami Marlins |
| Nick Gonzales | .304 | Pittsburgh Pirates |
| TJ Rumfield | .301 | Colorado Rockies |
Gonzales ranks fourth in the NL and is nine points behind Philadelphia Phillies second baseman Luis Arraez, who leads with a .315 batting average.
Arraez is always towards the top of the batting average leaderboards, winning three straight batting titles from 2022 to 2024, .316 with the Minnesota Twins in 2022, .354 with the Miami Marlins in 2023 and then .314 with both the Marlins and the Padres in 2024.
Moreno is having a career year, like Gonzales, and has never hit above .300 before. He's been excellent in September, batting .333/.410/.611 for a 1.021 OPS.
Lopez is also putting up his best season yet, and has bounced back from a poor August by hitting .316/.418/.404 for an OPS of .822 in September.
Rumfield has been great in his rookie season and at his very best this month, batting .408/.491/.633 for an OPS of 1.124.
Why Gonzales Winning Batting Title Means to Pirates
Gonzales has been a constant for the Pirates on the basepaths and someone they can rely on to get a rally going.
He hit his best in July, .388/.438/.544 for an OPS of .982, but has hit just .260/.352/.323 for an OPS of .675 since the start of August.
Gonzales needs to put up some great numbers to overtake Arraez and the other competition, but it's not impossible.
He's gotten more time at designated hitter than at third base, with his defensive struggles, but he's absolutely been an important part of the Pirates' offense.
"I hope he gets there and I hope he does it," Pirates manager Don Kelly said about Gonzales. "Awesome for him to be in the top of the batting order in the National League, and I hope that he can get up there and win it. He should take pride in that in how he's been able to swing the bat for us. He's had some huge at-bats, and swung the bat well and been a big part of our offensive success this year."
